title: India's EV Adoption Surges Past 10 Million as Public Charger Network Expands
excerpt: Electric vehicle penetration has jumped from 0.71% to 8.26% in six years, with the government targeting 72,000 new charging stations by FY28 under the PM E-DRIVE scheme.
body:
• India has crossed 10 million cumulative EV registrations, with electric vehicle penetration rising from 0.71% in FY20 to 8.26% in FY26.
  • Over 6,645 public charging stations are operational under FAME-II, with Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, and Maharashtra leading deployment.
  • The PM E-DRIVE scheme allocates ₹2,000 crore for 72,000+ new chargers by FY28, while fast chargers are replacing the slower units that make up 70% of the current network.
  • More than half of all new three-wheelers sold in India are now electric, and fleet operators are increasingly shifting to behind-the-meter depot charging.

India has hit a milestone in its electric mobility push: 10 million electric vehicles are now registered across the country, according to government data. The figure marks a dramatic acceleration from just five years ago, when EVs accounted for less than 1% of new vehicle sales.

EV penetration has climbed from 0.71% in FY20 to 8.26% in FY26, driven by a combination of government subsidies, falling battery costs, and a rapidly expanding charging infrastructure that is starting to address the range anxiety that held back early adoption.

Charging Infrastructure Takes Shape

Under the FAME-II (Faster Adoption and Manufacturing of Electric Vehicles) scheme, 6,645 public charging stations are now operational out of 9,332 sanctioned, with ₹912.50 crore allocated specifically for charging infrastructure. Across all programs, 29,151 charging stations have been installed across Indian states over the past five years.

Tamil Nadu leads with 957 operational stations, followed by Karnataka at 751 and Maharashtra at 670. The geographic spread matters — early charging infrastructure was concentrated in a handful of metros, leaving intercity routes underserved.

"The transition from slow to fast charging is critical. About 70% of existing stations are slow chargers, and the shift to DC fast charging will determine whether EVs work for mainstream buyers, not just early adopters."

— Industry analysts, per Livemint

The government's next-generation push comes through the PM E-DRIVE scheme, which allocates ₹2,000 crore to deploy over 72,000 new chargers by FY28. The program emphasizes fast-charging stations along highways and in tier-2 cities where current coverage is thin.

Three-Wheelers Lead the Shift

While passenger cars grab headlines, the real EV revolution in India is happening in the three-wheeler segment. Over 50% of new three-wheelers sold are now electric — a transformation driven by simple economics. For auto-rickshaw drivers and last-mile delivery operators, the per-kilometer cost of running an EV is a fraction of petrol or diesel.

Fleet operators are also reshaping the charging landscape. Rather than relying on public infrastructure, large logistics companies and ride-hailing platforms are building behind-the-meter depot charging facilities, where vehicles charge overnight at industrial electricity rates.

Challenges Remain

The 10 million milestone, while significant, comes with caveats. Two-wheelers dominate the count — electric scooters and motorcycles make up the vast majority of registrations, while four-wheeler EV adoption remains a small fraction of the overall car market.

Charging speed is another bottleneck. With 70% of existing public chargers being slow AC units, a full charge can take several hours. The planned shift to DC fast chargers under PM E-DRIVE is designed to address this, but deployment timelines have historically slipped.

"India's EV story is a two-speed narrative: two-wheelers and three-wheelers have crossed the tipping point, but four-wheelers still need another cycle of price parity and infrastructure buildout."

— EV industry observer, per Outlook Business

What's Next

The immediate focus is on execution. The PM E-DRIVE scheme's 72,000-charger target by FY28 is ambitious, and hitting it would roughly triple India's public charging network. Private investment from automakers and energy companies is accelerating alongside government spending, with Tata, Ather, and Reliance all expanding their charging footprints.

For the Indian diaspora watching from abroad, the pace of change is striking. Indian cities that were choking on auto-rickshaw exhaust a decade ago are now seeing electric three-wheelers outnumber their combustion counterparts — a shift that was barely imaginable five years ago.
